  • 11 Who is considered as the "Father of Botany"?
  • The ancient Greek scholar Theophrastus is known as the "Father of Botany"
  • 12 List any two applications of plant genetic engineering
  • Two applications of plant genetic engineering are improving crop traits like pest resistance and nutritional
  • value, and using plants as bioreactors to produce pharmaceuticals
  • 13 Explain the statement - all food comes from plants.
  • Plants are the foundation of nearly every food chain. Plants produce their own food through photosynthesis
  • using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to create energy. Humans and animals get energy directly by eating
  • plants, or indirectly by eating animals that have eaten plants.
  • Plants are the ultimate food source
  •  Directly: You eat food that comes directly from plants, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, nuts, and
  • seeds.
  •  Indirectly: Animals that eat other animals (carnivores and omnivores) still ultimately rely on plants.
  • In food chain - the energy captured in plants passes to the herbivores and then to carnivores. Similarly, milk
  • and eggs come from animals that consume plants, making those products indirectly plant-based.
  • 14 Discuss the evolutionary trends leading to the dominance of angiosperms in plant
  • diversity.
  • The dominance of angiosperms (flowering plants) is attributed to a suite of evolutionary innovations
  • particularly in their reproductive strategies, physiological efficiency, and ecological adaptability. These traits
  • provided significant advantages over gymnosperms and ferns, leading to their rapid diversification and global
  • spread.
  • Key evolutionary trends and innovations include
  •  Flowers and Animal Pollination
  •  Enclosed Ovules (Carpel)
  •  Fruits and Seed Dispersal
  •  Double Fertilization and Endosperm
  •  Efficient Vascular System
  •  Leaf Efficiency and Genome Size
  •  Growth Habit and Adaptability.
  •  Whole-Genome Duplications (WGDs)
  • (any five points with explanation in atleast one sentences – full mark)

  • Fig leaves hold significant importance in the diets of many lemur species, particularly as a consistent and
  • available food source that provides vital protein, especially during periods when preferred fruits are scarce.
  • Key Significance of Fig Leaves in Lemur Diets
  •  Nutritional Value: Fig leaves can provide essential nutrients, including protein
  •  Year-Round Availability (Fallback Food): different fig species mature asynchronously, ensuring a
  • more or less continuous supply of leaves and fruits throughout the year
  •  High Consumption Rates: Some lemur species, both their fruits and leavesare consumed in large
  • quantity
  •  Dietary Flexibility: The ability to switch between fruit-heavy and leaf-heavy diets depending on
  • seasonal availability
  •  Overcoming Plant Defenses: Plants often contain chemical deterrents like tannins and alkaloids.
  • Lemurs that consume fig leaves show adaptations or tolerances to process these secondary
  • compounds, though consumption might be limited past a certain threshold.
  •  Ecosystem Role: As major consumers of figs, lemurs play an important ecological role as seed
  • dispersers

  • Advantages of Pseudocopulation for Orchids
  •  Energy Efficiency: Unlike many flowering plants that produce nectar to attract pollinators, orchids

  •  Specialized Pollination: Pseudocopulation often results in species-specific pollination. The orchid is

  • between flowers of the same species. This reduces the risk of pollen being wasted on the wrong
  • species of flower, increasing the likelihood of successful fertilization.
  • 22 Describe the different types of microtomes and discuss their specific applications.
  • Microtomes slice samples into thin sections for microscopic examination, with different types designed
  • for specific applications, such as rotary for routine histology, cryostats for frozen samples, sliding for
  • large or hard blocks, and ultramicrotomes for ultra-thin sections required for electron microscopy. Other
  • types include vibrating microtomes for fresh, soft tissue and saw microtomes for extremely hard
  • materials like bone.
  • Types of microtomes and applications
  • Rotary microtome : The most common type, using a rotary motion to feed the sample towards a fixed
  • knife.
  •  Application: Routine histology and pathology labs for sectioning paraffin-embedded tissues.
  • Cryostat microtome (Cryomicrotome): A rotary microtome housed in a refrigerated chamber, typically
  • at -200C - -300C
  •  Application: Rapid sectioning of frozen tissue samples, often used in surgical pathology and
  • nerve biopsies.
  • Sliding microtome: The knife slides across a stationary block of tissue.
  •  Application: Sectioning large or particularly hard blocks of tissue, such as those embedded in
  • celloidin, or for materials like wood, bone, and teeth.
  • Vibrating microtome (Vibratome) :Uses a vibrating blade to cut samples.
  •  Application: Sectioning soft, fresh, or unfixed samples without freezing or embedding
  • minimizing damage to cell morphology.
  • Ultramicrotome : A specialized instrument for producing ultra-thin sections.
  •  Application: Preparing sections as thin as 40–100 nm for transmission electron microscopy
  • (TEM).
  • Saw microtome: Uses a saw for cutting.
  •  Application: Sectioning extremely hard and brittle materials like bone, teeth, and ceramics.
  • Laser microtome: A non-contact method that uses a laser to section samples.
  •  Application: Applications where a sample's cell morphology must remain unaltered, as it
  • eliminates physical contact and minimizes sample distortion.
  • (Explanation of rotary, sledge and ultra microtome - full mark)

  • 21 Give and account on the special adaptations in plants with reference to
  • the types to heliotropisim and pseudocopulation in orchids.
  • Plants have evolved sophisticated adaptations, such as heliotropism and pseudocopulation in orchids, to
  • optimize survival and reproductive success in diverse environments.
  • Heliotropism in Sunflowers
  • Heliotropism in sunflowers is a fascinating example of how plants have evolved to adapt to their environment
  • and can actively move to optimize their exposure to sunlight. Sunflowers, especially when they are young
  • exhibit a behavior called solar tracking, where their heads follow the movement of the sun across the sky
  • during the day. By following the sun, young sunflowers maximize their energy intake, promoting better growth
  • and ensuring reproductive success. Once mature, they continue to use their position to attract pollinators
  • completing the cycle of life.
  • East to West Movement
  •  During the day, young sunflower plants face the east to catch the rising sun. As the sun moves across
  • the sky, the sunflower’s stem slowly bends to track the sun’s path, turning from east to west. This
  • movement is driven by the differential growth of cells on the stem. The side facing away from the sun
  • grows faster, causing the plant to bend toward the light.
  •  At night, the sunflower "resets" by reorienting itself to face the east again.
  • Mechanism
  • The movement is controlled by the plant’s circadian rhythm, a natural internal clock that helps regulate its
  • daily movements. Auxins, a type of plant hormone, play a crucial role in this process. They accumulate on the
  • shaded side of the stem, promoting cell elongation, which causes the plant to bend toward the light.
  • Mature Sunflowers
  • Once sunflowers reach maturity and their large heads develop, they stop moving. At this stage, the flowers
  • generally remain facing east. It’s believed that east-facing sunflowers warm up more quickly in the morning
  • sun, making them more attractive to pollinators like bees, which prefer warmer flowers.
  • Benefits of Heliotropism in Sunflowers- Increased Photosynthesis: By tracking the sun, young sunflowers
  • can maximize the amount of sunlight they absorb throughout the day. This increases their ability to
  • photosynthesize, promoting faster growth and better energy production.

  • 22 Describe the different types of microtomes and discuss their specific applications.
  • Microtomes slice samples into thin sections for microscopic examination, with different types designed
  • for specific applications, such as rotary for routine histology, cryostats for frozen samples, sliding for
  • large or hard blocks, and ultramicrotomes for ultra-thin sections required for electron microscopy. Other
  • types include vibrating microtomes for fresh, soft tissue and saw microtomes for extremely hard
  • materials like bone.
  • Types of microtomes and applications
  • Rotary microtome : The most common type, using a rotary motion to feed the sample towards a fixed
  • knife.
  •  Application: Routine histology and pathology labs for sectioning paraffin-embedded tissues.
  • Cryostat microtome (Cryomicrotome): A rotary microtome housed in a refrigerated chamber, typically
  • at -200C - -300C
  •  Application: Rapid sectioning of frozen tissue samples, often used in surgical pathology and
  • nerve biopsies.
  • Sliding microtome: The knife slides across a stationary block of tissue.
  •  Application: Sectioning large or particularly hard blocks of tissue, such as those embedded in
  • celloidin, or for materials like wood, bone, and teeth.
  • Vibrating microtome (Vibratome) :Uses a vibrating blade to cut samples.
  •  Application: Sectioning soft, fresh, or unfixed samples without freezing or embedding
  • minimizing damage to cell morphology.
  • Ultramicrotome : A specialized instrument for producing ultra-thin sections.
  •  Application: Preparing sections as thin as 40–100 nm for transmission electron microscopy
  • (TEM).
  • Saw microtome: Uses a saw for cutting.
  •  Application: Sectioning extremely hard and brittle materials like bone, teeth, and ceramics.
  • Laser microtome: A non-contact method that uses a laser to section samples.
  •  Application: Applications where a sample's cell morphology must remain unaltered, as it
  • eliminates physical contact and minimizes sample distortion.
